items.headline: Anthropic hires the founder of Google's TPU program as it moves to design its own chips
items.body: Anthropic has hired Amir Salek, who founded and ran Google's custom AI chip program until 2022 and delivered the first seven generations of its tensor processing units, Bloomberg reported Friday. Salek joins Anthropic's compute team from the private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management and will report to James Bradbury. Anthropic currently buys silicon from Nvidia, Google and Amazon, and has been posting jobs for an in-house chip effort.
items.plain: A tensor processing unit is a chip built for one narrow job - the arithmetic behind training and running AI models - rather than the general-purpose work an ordinary processor does. Google built its own so it would not have to buy everything from Nvidia at Nvidia's price. Anthropic is the largest AI lab that still rents all of its silicon from other companies, and a chip takes roughly three to four years to go from design to working hardware. Hiring the person who did this at Google is the first visible step, not the result.
items.why: If every large model builder designs its own silicon, Nvidia's biggest customers become its competitors on a delay measured in years rather than quarters.

items.headline: Putin turns Russia's parliamentary election into a vote on continuing the war
items.body: At the United Russia party congress on Saturday, Vladimir Putin built the party's platform around the war in Ukraine and its expected victory in the coming State Duma elections, setting up that result as evidence that Russians support a protracted war, according to the Institute for the Study of War. He also acknowledged the damage Ukrainian long-range strikes have done to Russian fuel infrastructure and called for stronger air defenses. Russian attacks killed at least seven people in Ukraine on Saturday; Ukrainian strikes killed at least 10 in Russia and Moscow-occupied territory.
items.plain: The State Duma is Russia's lower house of parliament, and United Russia is the party Putin controls. Opposition parties capable of beating it are not permitted to run, so the outcome is known in advance. What Putin did on Saturday was attach a meaning to that outcome ahead of time: a win becomes proof the public chose the war. The unplanned part is the more revealing one. He had to concede on stage that Ukrainian drones are hitting Russian refineries and fuel depots often enough that a campaign speech had to address it.
items.why: Putin is manufacturing a domestic mandate for a war with no end date at the same moment he admits Ukraine can reach deep inside Russia.

sources.outlet: Institute for the Study of War via Kyiv Post

items.headline: Brent crude closes near $94 after a second straight weekly gain with Hormuz still shut
items.body: Brent crude settled at $94.39 a barrel on Friday, up roughly 6% on the week and posting a second consecutive weekly gain. Prices had fallen through the first half of August as US officials signalled a deal with Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was close; no agreement materialised, attacks on shipping continued and rhetoric hardened on both sides. Crude rose more than 2% after Trump threatened what he called an "economic D-Day" against Iran, and the administration is due to detail that sanctions package on Monday.
items.plain: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of sea between Iran and Oman that about a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. It has been closed since the war began, so tankers either wait or take much longer routes, and buyers bid up whatever crude is available elsewhere. Oil is an input to almost everything - fuel, fertiliser, plastics, shipping - so its price shows up in consumer prices with a lag of a few months. That lag is why an oil move in August becomes an interest-rate problem in the winter.
items.why: Energy near $94 takes away the Fed's room to cut rates just as tariffs and health costs push in the same direction.

items.headline: Employer health costs are projected to rise 9.5% next year, a fourth straight year near double digits
items.body: Aon projected this week that US employer health care costs will climb 9.5% in 2027, pushing the average above $19,000 per employee. The estimate draws on more than 1,100 employers covering 7.9 million people and $135 billion of 2026 health spending, and assumes companies make no changes to their benefits. Aon attributes the increase to higher use of care, rising rates of chronic illness, a growing number of very high-cost claims, and spending on specialty drugs and GLP-1 medicines.
items.plain: About half of Americans get health insurance through a job, and the employer pays most of the premium. When that bill grows faster than revenue, employers do not simply absorb it - they raise deductibles, narrow the list of covered doctors, or hold down raises. So a forecast about corporate budgets is really a forecast about your paycheck and what you owe at the front desk. Aon's 9.5% assumes employers do nothing, and Aon expects most of them to act. The acting is the part workers feel.
items.why: A fourth consecutive year near 10% makes employer coverage one of the most persistent sources of inflation left in the economy, and it sits almost entirely outside the Fed's reach.

items.headline: Dutch regulator fines Uber 825 million euros for suspending drivers by algorithm
items.body: The Dutch Data Protection Authority fined Uber 825 million euros ($966 million) in a decision dated August 17 and reported Friday, finding that the company deactivated driver accounts between 2018 and 2022 through automated decision-making, without adequate human review and without telling drivers a machine was deciding - a breach of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation. It is the second-largest GDPR penalty on record, behind Ireland's 1.2 billion euro fine against Meta in 2023. Uber said it "strongly disagree[s] with this decision and disproportionate fine" and will appeal.
items.plain: The GDPR is Europe's data protection law. One of its less-discussed clauses says a computer may not make a decision with a serious effect on your life unless a person can review it and you were told the machine was deciding. For a gig driver, losing the account is losing the income, so the regulator treated a deactivation as exactly that kind of decision. This case is not about data leaking out. It is about who is allowed to decide, which makes it relevant to any company automating decisions about people in Europe.
items.why: This attaches a billion-dollar price tag to algorithmic management at the moment companies are racing to hand more decisions to automated systems.

items.headline: Kazakhstan votes in the first election to its new single-chamber parliament
items.body: Kazakhstan voted on Sunday for the 145 seats of the Kurultai, the single-chamber legislature created by a constitution that took effect on July 1 and replaced the country's two-house parliament. Seven parties are running under nationwide proportional representation, and the newly formed, pro-presidential Adilet party is widely expected to win an overwhelming majority. Turnout reached 37.05% by noon, with 4,670,816 ballots issued. Nearly 80 parliamentarians and staff from about 30 countries are observing for the OSCE.
items.plain: Kazakhstan is the largest country in Central Asia, sits between Russia and China, and supplies a large share of the world's uranium along with a meaningful amount of its oil. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev rewrote the constitution to merge two chambers into one, and the party expected to fill the new chamber was created recently and backs him. Merging the chambers removes a body that could have slowed legislation down. The government calls this a democratic milestone; outside analysts call it consolidation. The OSCE observers' verdict, rather than the vote count, is the thing worth waiting for.
items.why: A more centralised Kazakhstan matters to both Moscow and Beijing, which depend on its pipelines and on its willingness to stay non-aligned.

items.headline: Bitcoin has its biggest week since 2024 after the Treasury expands bond buybacks
items.body: Bitcoin rose about 20% over the week, its largest weekly gain since March 2024, topping $75,000 on Friday for the first time since May and reaching roughly $79,500. CNBC put the weekly move at 22%; Bloomberg put it at almost 20%. The rally began after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the department would more than double its repurchases of long-dated government debt, and extended on Trump's push for the industry-backed CLARITY Act. Bitcoin ETFs took in $1.6 billion over the week, and about $1.21 billion of short positions were liquidated in 24 hours.
items.plain: When the Treasury buys back its own bonds, it hands cash to the investors who were holding them. That cash goes looking for a return, and some of it lands in the riskiest assets available. A short position is a bet that a price will fall; when the price rises instead, the bettor is forced to buy in order to close out, which pushes the price up further. So a large part of this move is mechanical rather than a judgment about bitcoin itself. The CLARITY Act would settle which US agency regulates which digital assets.
items.why: The same liquidity injection that failed to hold down government borrowing costs for even two days moved crypto 20%, which tells you where the money went instead.

items.headline: Mexico resumes cattle exports to the US as a yearlong screwworm ban ends
items.body: The US is reopening its border to Mexican cattle under tight controls, ending a ban of roughly a year imposed over the New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite. Shipments are capped at 700 head a day in the first week and 900 in the second, rising gradually toward 1,300. Mexico currently has 1,969 active screwworm cases, fewer than half the number reported a year ago. The cattle trade was worth $1.2 billion to Mexico last year.
items.plain: The New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae eat the living flesh of warm-blooded animals, cattle included. It was driven out of North America decades ago by releasing sterilised males, so matings produce no offspring, and it has worked its way back up through Central America. The US closed the border to keep it from crossing. Cutting off Mexican cattle made an American herd shortage worse at a time when beef was already at record prices, so this reopening is about grocery bills as much as animal health. But 700 head a day is a trickle against normal volumes.
items.why: US beef supply is being rationed by a parasite quarantine at the same time the administration is waiving beef tariffs to try to bring prices down.

items.headline: TikTok and ByteDance will pay $400 million to settle the US children's privacy case
items.body: The Justice Department announced Friday that TikTok, ByteDance and affiliated entities will pay $400 million to resolve litigation under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act - $300 million immediately and $100 million once a court vacates an earlier consent decree against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly. The government sued in 2024, alleging TikTok collected personal information from children under 13 without parental consent. The department called it among the largest COPPA recoveries ever obtained. TikTok did not admit wrongdoing.
items.plain: COPPA is a 1998 US law barring websites from collecting personal information from children under 13 without a parent's permission. A consent decree is a court-approved promise to fix a problem, and the government's argument was that TikTok had already broken one it inherited from Musical.ly, the app it absorbed. Notice how the money splits: a quarter of the total depends on a judge cancelling that old order, so TikTok is paying to clear its record as well as to close the case. Settling means no court ever rules on whether the law was broken.
items.why: The case that shadowed TikTok through its ownership fight ends with a payment and no finding of liability, which sets a price rather than a precedent.

items.headline: Trump says taxpayers are not paying for his ballroom; his contractor's own quote assigns them more than half
items.body: Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay on Friday letting construction of the White House ballroom continue, pausing an injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. A divided appeals court had held that Congress, not the president, has "full constitutional control over federal property and the funding of its maintenance and development." Trump said again on Saturday that taxpayers are not paying for the project, Forbes reported; in the Oval Office on March 31 he said, "This is taxpayer-free. We have no taxpayer putting up 10 cents." A Clark Construction summary presented to the White House in early March, obtained by The Washington Post, priced the job at $600 million: $293 million from private sources, $155 million from the Secret Service, $149 million from the White House Military Office and $3 million from the Executive Residence.
items.plain: The Secret Service, the White House Military Office and the Executive Residence are all funded by Congress out of tax revenue, so money spent through those accounts is taxpayer money by definition. That is what makes the contractor's arithmetic a direct contradiction rather than a difference of opinion. Trump has given three public totals over time - $200 million, then $300 million, then $400 million - while the builder's own estimate reached $600 million. The court case is not about the cost at all. It asks whether a president can demolish and rebuild part of the White House without Congress voting for it.
items.why: Roberts's order is temporary and settles nothing, but it lets the construction become a fact on the ground before the constitutional question is answered.
